definition: Vindicate means to clear someone from blame or show them to have been right, as later events or outside proof do.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word vindicate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know vindicate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The navigator's unfashionable detour around the shoals cost a day and drew jeers, but the wreck of a faster packet on those same rocks vindicated her course within the week.
Evidence may support a theory while the doubters still sneer; support stops far short of vindicate, which settles the argument in its author's favor.
To confirm a claim is to show it true; confirm stops short of vindicate, which also redeems the person who was mocked for making it.

To justify is to give reasons that make an action look reasonable — you can justify your own decision, in advance, and to yourself. Vindicate cannot be self-served: it waits for events or outside proof to show the doubted choice was right. Justification is argued; vindication arrives.

To uphold is to back a decision on review — an appeals board upholds a ruling, quietly confirming it was sound. Vindicate carries the drama uphold lacks: doubters proved wrong, a mocked judgment redeemed by events. Upholding is routine agreement from above; vindication is the world coming around.

Vindicate means to clear someone from blame or show them to have been right, as later events or outside proof do.

For twenty years the museum labeled the little portrait 'workshop copy,' overruling the assistant curator who had catalogued it as genuine; the restorer's discovery of the master's signature under the varnish vindicated her at last.
Vindicate does double duty: it clears a person of blame, and it proves a doubted judgment right.
That second sense is its signature — evidence can exculpate you of a crime, but only being proved correct can vindicate your decision.
Vindicate is the headline word for doubters proved wrong.

In this unit's clearing family, evidence exculpates, boards exonerate, authorities absolve — vindicate is what time and events do, and alone among them it can take your judgment, your gamble, or your theory as its object, not just you.

vindicate: To confirm a claim is to show it true; confirm stops short of vindicate, which also redeems the person who was mocked for making it.
When Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents drift, geology's establishment laughed him out of the lecture halls.
He was a meteorologist, they noted, an outsider with no mechanism to offer; textbooks of the era dismissed the idea in a footnote.
Wegener died on the Greenland ice in 1930, still collecting data, still mocked.
Then, in the 1960s, ocean-floor surveys revealed the seams where new crust spreads, and the mechanism no one could imagine turned out to be real.
The discovery vindicated Wegener completely: the drift he described was fact.
The scientists who had jeered were not consulted for the revision; the evidence itself overruled them, forty years too late for the man it proved right.
